hints: Think of the two different ways complexes with the same formula can differ in 3D space, one involving different positions around the metal and one involving non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Separate the two kinds of 3D difference**
Picture an octahedral or square planar complex. You can swap which ligand sits next to which, so cis versus trans positions give one family. Separately, you can have a chiral arrangement like a propeller that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, which gives the second family.

Final answer: 1. cis-trans / geometrical isomerism
2. optical isomerism

hints: Recall which 4-coordinate geometry allows cis and trans positions, and why a bidentate $en$ ligand $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ can only span adjacent positions.
walkthrough:
Use the isomer count to pick the shape**
$\text{[Pt(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{Cl}_2\text{]}$ has two forms, cis with the two $\text{Cl}$ next to each other and trans with the two $\text{Cl}$ opposite each other. That pattern is classic for $\text{Pt(II)}$, which is $d^8$ and 4-coordinate square planar. In $\text{[Pt(}en\text{)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ each $en$ is bidentate and must occupy two cis positions, so the chelate ring locks out the trans alternative and only one structure is possible.

hints: Visualise octahedral $\text{[Cr(AB)}_3\text{]}$ where $\text{AB} = {}^{-}\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ with O at one end and N at the other, so swapping O and N ends creates new geometries.
Remember that symmetrical $\text{[Cr(}en\text{)}_3\text{]}^{2+}$ shows only one geometric type with a pair of enantiomers, while an unsymmetrical ligand adds a fac versus mer distinction.

Think of fac as three O atoms on one triangular face (all O cis) and mer as three O atoms around the meridian (two O trans), each existing as a non-superimposable mirror image pair to give four in total.
walkthrough:
See why this ligand doubles the count**
$en$, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, is symmetrical, both ends are N, so $\text{[Cr(}en\text{)}_3\text{]}^{2+}$ has only the propeller chirality, delta and lambda, two optical isomers. Here the ligand is $^{-}\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{NH}_2$, O at one end and N at the other. Flipping a chelate so O and N swap ends now matters.

Build the fac family**
Put all three O donors on one face of the octahedron. That means every O is cis to every other O, and similarly every N is cis to every other N. This arrangement is chiral like a three-bladed propeller, so it exists as two enantiomers. Draw two mirror image octahedra with the three O ends clustered together, one right handed and one left handed.

Build the mer family**
Now arrange the three O donors around the meridian, so two O atoms are trans to each other across Cr while the third is cis. The N atoms are likewise meridional. This is geometrically different from fac and is also chiral, so it also exists as a pair of enantiomers. Draw two further mirror image octahedra with one O trans O linkage clearly shown.

Check you have four distinct 3D drawings**
You should finish with four structures: fac delta, fac lambda, mer delta-like and mer lambda-like. No two should be superimposable by rotation. Each uses three O-N arcs joining adjacent positions, never spanning trans positions because the bidentate bite is too short.

Final answer: Four octahedral stereoisomers: fac pair of enantiomers (all three O cis, all three N cis) and mer pair of enantiomers (two O trans, two N trans). Drawn with O-N arc for $^{-}\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ linking adjacent octahedral positions in the four distinct O/N arrangements.

hints: Identify the nucleophile in $\text{H}_3\text{N:}$ and the electrophilic carbon in oxirane, remembering the $\text{C-O}$ bond is polarised by the electronegative O.
Think about which two electron pairs move when the ring opens, one to form the new $\text{N-C}$ bond and one to break a $\text{C-O}$ bond onto O.
Consider the charges that result when neutral ammonia forms a new bond and when O gains the $\text{C-O}$ bonding electrons.
walkthrough:
Spot the nucleophile and electrophile**
Ammonia $\text{H}_3\text{N:}$ has a lone pair, so it is the nucleophile. In oxirane, O pulls electrons away from C, so each C is $\delta+$ and O is $\delta-$. Mark that $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$ dipole. The lone pair on N will be attracted to either equivalent $\text{CH}_2$ carbon.

Push the two arrows for ring opening**
Draw one curly arrow starting at the N lone pair and pointing to a C atom of the epoxide to make the new $\text{N-C}$ bond. Draw a second curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C-O}$ bond on that same carbon and pointing onto the O atom. That breaks the three-membered ring and puts the bonding electrons onto O.

Work out the intermediate charges**
Neutral $\text{NH}_3$ uses its lone pair to form a fourth bond, so N becomes $+1$: $-\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_3$. The O gains an extra electron pair and loses one bond, so it becomes $-1$: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{O}^{-}$. The organic intermediate is therefore $^{+}\text{H}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}$. In step 2 proton transfer gives neutral $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from N lone pair of $\text{NH}_3$ to C of oxirane; curly arrow from $\text{C-O}$ bond to O; $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown; intermediate $^{+}\text{H}_3\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}$ (2-aminoethoxide zwitterion).

hints: Compare the nucleophilicity of the product $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ with ammonia and think about what happens if product meets more oxirane.
walkthrough:
Block the second attack**
The product 2-aminoethanol still has a lone pair on N, so it can act as a nucleophile toward another oxirane molecule to give E, $\text{(HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{NH}$. If ammonia molecules hugely outnumber product molecules, an oxirane is far more likely to collide with $\text{NH}_3$ than with product, so formation of E is minimised.
Final answer: Use an excess of ammonia (or use a limiting amount of oxirane).

hints: Compare formulae $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_2$ for E and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{NO}$ for F to find what small molecule is lost.
Think how a molecule with two $\text{-OH}$ groups and one $\text{-NH-}$ group can join its ends with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give a saturated basic ring containing both N and O.
walkthrough:
Deduce loss of water and cyclisation**
Subtract the formulae: $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_2$ minus $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{NO}$ equals $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong dehydrating agent. E is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. One $\text{-OH}$ can be protonated and leave as water while the O of the other end attacks, closing a six-membered ring.

Draw F and name the reaction type**
Join the two carbon chains through O and NH to make a saturated heterocycle with four $\text{CH}_2$ groups, one O and one secondary amine NH, that is morpholine. It is still basic because of the amine lone pair, and saturated because there are no $\text{C=C}$ bonds. This is an intramolecular elimination, also accepted as dehydration or condensation.

Final answer: F is morpholine, a six-membered ring $\text{O(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{NH}$ (O at position 1, NH at position 4); type of reaction: elimination / dehydration / condensation (intramolecular).
